IMPLEMENTATION REVIEW

26 Oct 2026 · 15 current branch snapshots

How the scores work

These are editorial judgments about the implementations at the linked commits, including later fixes. They are not measurements of model capability or ratings of the original one-shot commits.

Each category is scored from 0 to 10. Overall is their arithmetic mean, rounded to one decimal. Cards sort by that displayed overall score, then prompt completeness, then game design. Scores around 9 indicate strong implementation with minor gaps; 7–8 indicates a solid result with material weaknesses; 4–6 indicates a partial game; 0–3 indicates fundamental blockers or unfinished systems.

Game design
Playability, fairness, feedback, pacing, visual readability, and how the mall and store mechanics work together.
Code architecture
Separation of rules and presentation, state ownership, determinism, module boundaries, and integration between systems.
Code design
Algorithms, data models, APIs, collision and input handling, correctness, and how easily the implementation can be extended.
Code cleanliness
Readability, naming, formatting, duplication, useful comments, type discipline, and removal of unfinished or disconnected code.
Prompt completeness
Working coverage of the original prompt: traversal, packages, stores, enemies, extras, power-ups, screens, audio, art, input, and technical constraints.

Review scope

The review compared source, assets, tests, build configuration, and gameplay rules with the original prompt. Every implementation's test suite and production build was run. Haiku 4.5 also received a separate TypeScript check because its build does not typecheck.

Browser checks sampled launch, title, arrival, and mall presentation. Stronger implementations also received store-entry checks using prepared player positions; Fable, GPT-6.1, Haiku 5.5 and the two Sonnet 5.5 advisor entries received package-search checks, and GPT-6 Astra a fixture-search check. Haiku 5.5 was also played in real time through elevator boarding, the map and pause, then stepped through an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over. The Sonnet 5.5 + Fable 5.1 entry was played in real time on its published sub-path build through the arrival, walking, an elevator ride, the CRT and mute toggles, the map and pause, then its own scripted player, kept invulnerable, was driven through the complete six-package route to level clear, loop 2, continue, game over, the Konami code and the GameStonk easter egg; that run proves routing and screen flow rather than survivability. The Sonnet 5.5 + Opus 5.5 entry was played the same way on its published build, and its own scripted bot, left vulnerable, completed the six-package route to level clear and loop 2 on seed 5 without a death, matching the Node trajectory frame for frame; continue, game over, the Konami code, the GameStonk cave, an escalator ride and a lamp shot were stepped afterwards. Those are the only two verified full-route completions. GPT-6 Astra was stepped through its debug hook on the published build from splash to loop 2, including a store search, the kiosk, the photo booth, the fountain, the wet floor, the mall cop, death, continue, game over, the Konami code, the GameStonk cave and the sprite gallery, but was not played in real time. Kimi K3.1 Pro (high) was played in real time on its published build in headless Chrome driven over the DevTools protocol, because the Claude-in-Chrome extension was not connected: splash, title, the Konami code, the zip-line arrival, an elevator ride, a store entry with single-tap searches and a package, the map, pause, the CRT and mute toggles and the GameStonk cave; level clear was reached from a package count set by hand, then the newspaper, the post, loop 2, continue, game over and the gallery followed. Targeted probes reproduced the Haiku 4.5 timing blocker, the Gemini store-exit blocker, and the Haiku 5.5 map-in-store, floor-blind wet-floor, power-up timer and Game Over shutter defects; the Sonnet 5.5 + Fable 5.1 entry's silent cleared-store door and Black Friday title overlap were reproduced in the browser; the Sonnet 5.5 + Opus 5.5 entry's roof respawn after a death inside an elevator car was seen in real-time play and reproduced in Node. GPT-6 Sol's dead-spy and Black Friday defects were reproduced in Node; GPT-6 Astra's banner over the store header, package pose after an empty search and clipped Black Friday title sign were seen in stepped screenshots. The Kimi entry's fall through a rising car roof was reproduced in the live build and on a natural route in Node, its roof-pit death on the first walk right was counted over 40 seeds, and its photo-booth spy-contact death was reproduced in Node.

DeepSeek V4 Pro (high) was reviewed on its local Vite development server because its production build failed TypeScript checking, also blocking GitHub Pages deployment. Real-time keyboard checks with the default CRT covered splash, title, arrival, selfie, walking, the elevator boarding softlock, ordinary store entry immediately returning to the mall, map, pause and Konami input. A package search required placing the player beside a fixture and removing guards. Prepared package and life counts exercised level clear, newspaper, mission post, loop 2, continue and game over. Isolated rule probes reproduced the elevator and store-entry blockers, frozen store power-up timers, reset fixtures, repeated GameStonk rewards, retained packages in loop 2, roof respawn on continue, non-firing store spies, Black Friday loot gaps and keyboard/gamepad merging defects. Screenshots were inspected; no game JavaScript exception was observed, but the dev server returned favicon 404s. Music was not assessed by ear.

This was not an uninterrupted six-package walkthrough of all 15 games; the two full routes that were replayed are named above. Unverified full-route completion is not claimed for the others. Test counts are reported as context; they do not determine scores. Other findings come from source inspection and are described as inferences where relevant. Scores describe these source snapshots; published Play builds may change independently. The "written" date on each card is the day the model produced the implementation, taken from the branch README's benchmark notes or, where a README has none, from the branch's first commit.

Written 8 Oct 2026 · snapshot 94755064ac81 · branch sonnet-5-5-fable-5-1

Game design
Clean, readable storefronts with a wide corridor palette, a legible HUD with an LED floor panel and scrolling store marquee, and well-staged screens: a SPYGRAM card, a receipt-style tally, THE DAILY MALL, a vector-grid continue countdown and typewriter shutters at game over. Elevators glide, floor banners announce, the directory map is clear and shows the current store from inside a room. Fairness was tuned with scripted players over 40 seeds, not with a human. A cleared or closed store door gives no feedback on Up, and the Black Friday flash overlaps the copyright line on the title. Survivability by a human was not tested here.
Code architecture
A scene machine (Game) owns a Level that holds the mall, the current store, the overlays and the fades, so the map and pause work identically in both views. Rules are pure and frame-based, emit sound requests through the Run and expose music through state; a grep test keeps the rule layers free of the DOM, Math.random and timers. Mall extras (lamps, janitor, walkers, cop, kiosks, booth, fountains) are plug-in modules with typed state the renderer reads, which keeps the core world smaller than its siblings. The mall and store worlds are still about 1,200 lines each.
Code design
The elevator model (drive, glide, call protection, occupancy, grate and pit states), shaft-wall door windows, tile collision with corner assist, a tap queue that preserves fast taps across catch-up steps, and a store room system that already supports any size with a camera are all well modelled and tested. A scripted player that only presses buttons doubles as a routing proof and a fairness probe. Spy AI is deliberately simple, the cop ignores escalators, and a few interactions fall through silently.
Code cleanliness
Strict TypeScript with no escape hatches, no stray TODOs or console calls, every line of copy in one module with fit tests, named constants for all timings, and comments that explain gameplay decisions. The README and AGENTS.md are precise about what was and was not verified. There is no lint or format configuration and unused locals are not flagged, and the two world modules are long.
Prompt completeness
Every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, and 754 tests cover rules, art contracts, music theory and seeded playthroughs. This review drove the branch's own scripted player, kept invulnerable, through the whole route in the published sub-path build, which proves routing and screen flow rather than survivability: splash, title, arrival, walking, an elevator ride and escalator, a lamp shot, all six package stores, the refused re-entry of a cleared store, the exit firing once, the tally, newspaper and post, a harder loop 2, continue, game over, the Konami code and the GameStonk easter egg, with an empty console. Music was checked numerically by the author and not listened to here.

Verification

  • 754 tests passed.
  • Build: Pass; strict typecheck included.
  • Runtime: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator ride, floor banner, CRT and mute toggles, map and pause passed on the published build; stepped checks with the scripted player kept invulnerable completed the full six-package route to level clear, loop 2, continue, game over, Konami, easter egg, map inside a store, escalator and lamp shot with no console messages.

Written 9 Oct 2026 · snapshot aca8cc817c2e · branch sonnet-5-5-opus-5-5

Game design
Clean pastel storefronts whose windows read at a glance, a wide corridor palette, a 16 px HUD with an LED floor panel and a store marquee, a floor banner on every stop, and well-staged screens: the SPYGRAM card, a MISSION COMPLETE drive-off with the receipt-waving spy, a receipt-style tally, THE DAILY MALL and a typewriter message that stays readable over the game-over shutters. Searching is forgiving, with a progress bar under the store name. Fairness was tuned with a non-dodging bot over 24 seeds, and the same bot finished loop 1 on seed 5 in the live build without a death. The safe spot is never updated while riding, so a death inside an elevator car respawns the agent where it boarded; in real-time play a death at 2F sent the agent back to the roof. Checkerboard store floors are busier than the mall.
Code architecture
A Game state machine owns a RunState shared by the mall and the stores, a Mall and a StoreRoom; the map and pause remember which view is underneath, power-up timers tick in both views and stop on the overlays. The rules layer has no DOM, timers or Math.random, by inspection rather than a guard test, and emits plain events through one queue; the renderer keeps its own door, popup and toast state clocked by simulation frames, so visuals do not depend on the display refresh rate. Spies and NPCs are split out of the 1,300-line mall module and the store room system takes any size with a camera. Event payloads are untyped and consumers cast them.
Code design
The elevator model (glide, one ding per stop, call protection, grate, pit and roof states), the input mapper with printed-letter bindings, exact release and a tap queue, tile collision with corner assist, once-per-volley spy dodges, lamps placed by computing the corridor gaps from the geometry, and a goal-based BFS bot that doubles as a softlock detector are all well modelled and tested. The safe-spot rule ignores elevator rides, spy AI is simple, the cop ignores escalators, and one hazard check carries an empty branch.
Code cleanliness
Strict TypeScript, every line of copy in one module with fit tests, named frame constants, comments that explain decisions, and a README and AGENTS.md that record the advisor consultations and the gotchas. Unused locals are not flagged, so a dozen void statements silence unused imports; event data is typed as any, there is a placeholder draw call and an empty if block, and there is no lint or format configuration.
Prompt completeness
Every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, and 240 tests cover rules, input layouts, art contracts, songs, copy fit, refresh-rate timing, a 24-seed fairness run and a scripted full level on 8 seeds. This review played the published sub-path build in real time through splash, title, arrival, walking, an elevator ride, the map, pause and the CRT and mute toggles, then drove the branch's own scripted bot, left vulnerable, through the full six-package route on seed 5 to level clear, THE DAILY MALL, the post and loop 2 with no deaths, matching the Node trajectory frame for frame; continue, game over, the Konami code, the GameStonk cave, the map inside a store, an escalator ride and a lamp shot were stepped, with an empty console. Music was not listened to.

Verification

  • Build: Pass; strict typecheck included.
  • Runtime: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator ride, floor banner, map, pause, CRT and mute toggles passed on the published build; the branch's scripted bot, left vulnerable, completed the full six-package route to level clear and loop 2 with no deaths; continue, game over, Konami, GameStonk cave, map inside a store, escalator and lamp shot stepped with no console messages; the roof respawn after a death inside a car was seen live and reproduced in Node.

Written 9 Oct 2026 · snapshot 483c7038c153 · branch gpt-6-astra

Game design
The mall reads well at NES scale: every storefront shows its goods in the windows, blinking red doors mark the targets, closed shops carry FOR LEASE and CLOSING SALE shutters, floors are labelled, and the elevator cars have doors that close while moving. The title screen, the SPYGRAM cards, the kiosk panel, the photo strip, MISSION COMPLETE with the receipt-waving spy, THE DAILY MALL and the shutters rolling down over the mall at game over are all staged with care. The stores let it down: all ten rooms are the same 16 by 11 checkerboard with eight identical fixture boxes topped by one sprite per theme, no counters or walls, and two guards at fixed positions, so the Zelda half of the game is a flat grid. Music is one monophonic eight-note loop per track over a bass and a triangle, so the ten store songs are barely distinguishable. The banner box covers the store name header, the agent holds a package overhead after an empty or trapped search, and the Black Friday sign on the title is clipped by the storefront row.
Code architecture
A 1,782-line rules module owns the whole simulation as a plain state object stepped at 60 Hz with the state's own xorshift PRNG and no DOM, timers or Math.random; it emits events that the audio layer consumes, and the renderer only reads state. The fixed loop caps catch-up at five steps, the input layer merges keyboard and gamepad into held and pressed sets with a tap queue that survives catch-up, and the browser adapter is 175 lines. The room system clamps a camera to the room size, so bigger rooms would work, but nothing else is modular: mall, store, elevators, NPCs, lamps, scoring and screens all share one file, and the renderer imports the rules module to ask which fixture is touched.
Code design
The elevator model (floor-to-floor glide, one ding per stop, called cars that pick up instead of crush, the automatic car waiting for an occupant), the printed-letter input mapping with release by physical key, the forgiving touch-based search and the once-per-volley spy dodge are modelled cleanly and each has a test. Against that, the code is terse to a fault: state, player, elevator and fixture are s, p, e and f throughout, positions such as the wagon at 626, the booth at 410 and the kiosks at 384 are bare literals, and fixture contents are chosen by a ternary nested five deep. The search pose is reused for every outcome, which is why the agent lifts a package he did not find.
Code cleanliness
Prettier-style formatting is consistent, every line of copy sits in one module with a fit test, and the README and AGENTS.md are short and honest, including the note that the run began inside an existing conversation rather than a fresh session. There is no type checking, no lint configuration and almost no commenting, and the single-letter naming makes the rules file hard to scan. Tests are 56 broad cases in two files, several asserting a dozen things each.
Prompt completeness
Every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option in the brief is present, and 56 tests cover the fixed step, input layouts, the art pipeline, room reachability, elevators, scoring, power-up timers, NPCs, the Konami code, spy fairness, searching, the extras, the exit rule, continues, splash timing and copy limits. This review stepped the published sub-path build through its debug hook with the CRT on: splash, title, arrival and selfie, an elevator ride with its floor banner, a store visit with the first-visit lines, a search, the map and pause, a spy kill with last words, a falling lamp, an escalator, the kiosk, the photo booth, the fountain, the wet floor, the mall cop's detention, death and respawn, continue, game over, the Konami code and Black Friday signs, the GameStonk cave, the parking level, level clear, the newspaper, the post, loop 2, the CRT and mute toggles and the sprite gallery, with an empty console. Real-time keyboard play and the music were not checked by this review; the branch README reports its own real-time run. Store themes differ only by palette, Circuit Pity shows FOR LEASE instead of a half-open shutter, and guards are always two.

Verification

  • 56 tests passed.
  • Build: Pass; no dependencies, static copy to dist/.
  • Runtime: The published build was stepped through the debug hook with the CRT on: splash, title, arrival, selfie, elevator ride, store entry, search, map, pause, spy kill, lamp, escalator, kiosk, photo booth, fountain, wet floor, cop, death, continue, game over, Konami and Black Friday, GameStonk cave, level clear, newspaper, post, loop 2, CRT and mute toggles and the gallery, with no console messages; the banner over the store header, the package pose on an empty search and the clipped Black Friday sign were seen in screenshots. Real-time keyboard play was not exercised by this review.

Written 8 Oct 2026 · snapshot 1ec98345999f · branch haiku-5-5

Game design
The whole loop plays: zip-line arrival, elevators and escalators, timed searches with a progress bar, banners and popups, first-visit lines, level clear and harder loops, with telegraphed shots, store grace and respawn invulnerability for fairness. Opening the map inside a store leaves the room frozen on screen while the mall rules keep moving the agent, the wet-floor slide applies on every floor and can block the getaway wagon, timed power-ups never run out, and the Game Over screen ends fully covered by its shutters. Dark backdrops, abstract window displays and overflowing two-line signs make the mall less readable than the strongest entries.
Code architecture
Pure, seeded rules in core, mall and store modules emit typed events that a state-reading renderer and an audio layer consume; the input mapper and the splash are standalone and the browser shell is thin. The roughly 1,450-line mall module concentrates most behaviour, the game never ticks the power-up timers it owns, the map screen ignores which screen opened it, and banners persist across scene changes. Debug mode pauses real time, so the hooks cannot observe live play.
Code design
The elevator state machine, printed-letter input with exact key release and a tap queue, tile collision with corner assist, and once-per-volley dodge rolls are well modelled. The wet-floor check ignores floors, closing the map inside a store returns to the mall with the room still attached, timed power-ups last until death, the shutter animation covers the Game Over text, and the room system is fixed at 16 by 11 tiles without a camera.
Code cleanliness
Strict TypeScript with no escape hatches, short focused modules outside the mall world, readable names, and comments that explain gameplay decisions. Copy is duplicated inside rule modules despite the stated single-source rule, several sound effects, the shake output and some copy constants are defined but never used, and the README contradicts itself about the browser playtest.
Prompt completeness
Nearly every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, with 115 tests across the listed rule areas; the strict build and the published sub-path deployment work, and browser checks logged no console errors. Real-time play covered splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, the map, pause and the CRT and mute toggles; stepped checks covered store entry, a package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over. The unticked power-up timers, the map inside stores, the floor-blind wet patch and the hidden Game Over text are working-coverage gaps; the room camera, photo strip and automatic-car ride are simplified.

Written 24 Oct 2026 · snapshot a42596e3a4a7 · branch kimi-k3-1-pro-high

Game design
The screen flow is staged with care: the FLICKERSOFT flicker, a night-sky title, the zip line onto the roof, a SPYGRAM selfie card with climbing likes, floor banners on every elevator stop, a parking-garage tally with the receipt-waving spy, THE DAILY MALL, the mission post and shutters rolling down at game over. Play breaks down in the elevator shafts. A drop into a pit with the car one floor below lands the agent on its roof, but the roof is not tracked as a platform: when the car rises, and the brief's half-second auto-call raises it as soon as the agent stands still there, the agent falls through it and keeps falling forever with no death. That happens on a natural route (ride B from 4F to 3F, take the escalator back up, walk to B and wait), and the only escape is pressing Up blind at an open store door on that floor. Shaft B is drawn behind the Forever 12, KGB Toys and Sam Baddy facades, so its pit is invisible on 4F to 2F. Walking right from the start toward elevator A drops the agent into automatic car C's pit on the roof in 28 of 40 seeds, and jumping cannot clear an opening, so most first walks end in a death. Hiding in the photo booth does not protect from spy contact, standing in car C's open doorway is a crush when it leaves downward, and spies spawn at store doors anywhere on an adjacent floor, so four can be waiting on 4F before the agent leaves the roof. Store rooms are one 16 by 11 grid of identical boxes with a few rows moved per store; both windows of a storefront show the same display; two-line signs collide with the Black Friday banner, the 3F kiosk is drawn over Blockbluster's shutter and the newspaper's column rules run past the page.
Code architecture
The rules live in src/core as plain modules with no DOM, Canvas, timers or Math.random: one seeded xorshift stream, frame counters for every duration, a fixed-step accumulator capped at five catch-up steps, and events as the only route to sound and screen effects. Elevators, physics, searching, power-ups, scoring, input and copy are separate small modules, and the store renderer clamps a camera to the template size. The 899-line MallGame class still owns the mall, the stores, NPCs, lamps, screens and the scene machine in one place; main.js writes the CRT and sound notices into the rules state, and the renderer imports a rules helper it never uses.
Code design
The input pad releases the exact physical token, queues taps across catch-up steps and maps letters by printed key; elevator stops ding once on the moving-to-stopped edge, called cars do not crush their caller, and the Konami detector forgives leading Ups. The shaft logic is where it fails: the pit check re-arms every frame, the landing height follows the car only while the agent is over the opening, and integrateVertical lands only when the feet cross the target from above, so once a rising car passes the agent's feet no landing line is ever crossed again; stepping off a roof sideways snaps the agent back up to the floor it fell from. fallStartY means the head on a jump and the feet on a pit drop. Spy contact ignores the hidden flag, the automatic car counts only a boarded rider as an occupant, the cop teleports to the agent's floor every two seconds, and corner assist is a one-pixel nudge while the exported cornerAssist helper goes unused.
Code cleanliness
Modules are short and named for what they do, every line of copy sits in copy.js with fit tests, and the README, AGENTS.md and DECISIONS.md are honest about how the run went and what the playtest shortcuts. The two largest files pack several statements per line, with 41 lines over 180 characters in game.js and renderer.js; there are no types, no lint and few comments, a ternary that returns square either way, and unused exports (EVENT, approach, floorAtY, STORE_W, HUD_H, cornerAssist). The pages workflow still lists main as a trigger branch. Tests are 64 compact cases in six files.
Prompt completeness
Every screen, the Konami code with Black Friday, the map with car positions and radar marks, pause, continues, game over, the gallery, the debug hooks, the kiosks, photo booth, fountains, lamps and disco balls, janitor, walkers, cop, the fitting room, toy shelf, listening booth and GameStonk cave are present, and 64 tests cover most of section 11. Missing or thin: the 1-Up never appears (no shop or spy drop holds one, 0 of 33,034 fixtures over 199 seeds), riding a car roof does not work, spies never wait at shaft openings, there is no elevator hum, the kiosk answers with a text line instead of a map panel and the photo strip is a message. All ten store songs are one eight-note arpeggio transposed per store, several effects use a sawtooth outside the NES channel set, and the music was not listened to. This review drove the published sub-path build in headless Chrome over the DevTools protocol, in real time with key events and the CRT on: splash, title, Konami code, zip line, selfie, a death in car C's roof pit, calling C, boarding A and riding it to the 4F banner, a lost life on 4F of unrecorded cause, Radioshock entry, single-tap searches through a trap, a Spread Shot, a NOTHING HERE and the package, the map, pause, CRT and mute toggles, the GameStonk cave and its joke item, the blocked exit, then level clear from six packages set by hand, the newspaper, the post, loop 2, continue, game over and the gallery, with an empty console. No spy kill or lamp shot was confirmed live.

Verification

  • 64 tests passed.
  • Build: Pass; Vite production build, no runtime dependencies.
  • Runtime: The published build was played in real time in headless Chrome over the DevTools protocol with the CRT on (the Claude-in-Chrome extension was not connected): splash, title, Konami, arrival and selfie, a roof-pit death, an elevator ride with its banner, store entry, searches and a package, map, pause, CRT and mute, the GameStonk cave, the exit rule, level clear from a prepared package count, newspaper, post, loop 2, continue, game over and gallery, with no console messages; the fall-through after landing on a car roof was reproduced live and on a natural route in Node, and the photo-booth death and the 28-of-40-seed roof-pit death in Node.

Written 26 Oct 2026 · snapshot 5e524e1d4c84 · branch deepseek-v4-pro-high

Game design
The splash, title, zip-line arrival and selfie establish the premise, but ordinary progression is blocked. In real-time keyboard play, boarding elevator A left the agent at the roof: holding Down never moved the car, and Right could not leave it. After preparing a position at Forever 12, pressing Up entered the store for one simulation frame and immediately returned to the mall, even with Up held. The player spawns on the exit tile and cannot move far enough off it before the exit check. A package could be searched only after moving the player beside its fixture through the debug state and removing guards. Storefront windows are plain rectangles, signs are truncated to ten characters, and all store palettes fall back to the same gadget theme because the renderer looks up a store ID in a theme-keyed table. Screenshots show a clipped floor HUD and a black pause screen instead of a dimmed scene. These are fundamental playability and presentation gaps, rather than a difficult but complete game.
Code architecture
The strongest part is a real separation between pure seeded rules, Canvas drawing, browser input and Web Audio. Game owns session state and dispatches to separate mall and store modules; the renderer reads state and events drive sound. The fixed 60 Hz accumulator caps catch-up at five steps. However, event names and payloads are loosely typed, nearly all mall behavior shares one large module, and power-up ownership is split awkwardly: effects live on the mall player while the store has a different player and never advances those timers. Store state is recreated on every entry, so there is no durable per-level room state or per-game visit history. The module boundaries are useful, but missing integration prevents several declared systems from functioning.
Code design
Manual elevator input never sets a destination or movement direction, no code handles leaving a boarded car, and automatic-car updates do not carry the rider. The store spawn/exit geometry is incompatible. Probes also confirmed that a 1,200-frame weapon timer remains at 1,200 after 120 store steps, opened fixtures reset on re-entry, the GameStonk reward is granted again on every entry, and an aligned store spy stays at aim timer 30 for 240 frames without firing. Loop 2 retains all six collected packages and therefore keeps target stores cleared; level clear adds another 3,000 package points after collection already awards them. Continuing recreates the mall at the roof instead of resuming where the agent fell. Black Friday still generates traps and empty fixtures. Printed-letter keyboard mapping and physical-key release tracking work in isolation, but an idle connected gamepad clears keyboard-held buttons, and disconnecting a held gamepad leaves them stuck. Jumping has no horizontal movement while airborne, Spread Shot's normal two-bullet cap truncates its three shots, player bullets never trigger falling lamps, and spy-contact/jump-kick collisions are absent.
Code cleanliness
Names, formatting, section comments and explicit TypeScript state interfaces make the source substantially easier to inspect than compressed prototype entries. The dependency footprint is small and DECISIONS.md candidly lists some omissions. There is nevertheless considerable unfinished scaffolding: identical walk/jump sprite frames, unused store-extra fields, an identical-result bot sprite ternary, and comments claiming behavior that is not wired. Copy is not fully centralized. The suite has 60 passing cases, but its reachability test checks a graph of declared floors rather than operating elevators, and search tests move the player directly to fixtures, bypassing the broken entrance. The README's successful-build and complete-core-loop claims are contradicted by this snapshot: strict compilation fails in test/copy.test.ts:16 (possibly undefined line) and test/sprites.test.ts:52 (implicit-any callback parameter), matching the failed CI run.
Prompt completeness
There are thirteen storefront definitions, room layouts, seeded loot, scoring and power-up APIs, a map, pause, Konami detection, continue/game-over screens and the level-clear/headline/post sequence. Those pieces do not produce the required start-to-finish game: elevator travel and ordinary store entry are blocked, and the production build cannot deploy. Missing or partial systems include elevator calls, roof riding and crushing, store spy shooting, fitting rooms, wind-up toys, listening booths, the full GameStonk cave, fountain coin creation, photo strips, wet-floor sliding, walker penalties, working lamp shots/disco balls, radar marks, animated shop displays and the getaway-car scene. Store music is one shared eight-note pattern; the splash is embedded in Game/Renderer rather than a reusable module; CRT curvature is absent. Real-time browser checks used the local development server, not a published or production build. Prepared state reached one package and the closing screens; no full route is claimed. No game JavaScript exception was observed, but favicon requests returned 404s. The gallery and CRT/mute controls were sampled; music was inspected in source, not listened to.

Verification

  • Build: FAIL: tsc --noEmit reports TS18048 in test/copy.test.ts:16 and TS7006 in test/sprites.test.ts:52; Vite production bundling and Pages deployment are blocked. GitHub Actions run 40401003618 reports the same errors.
  • Runtime: Local Vite server, seed 5, real-time Playwright keyboard input with default CRT: splash, title, arrival, selfie, movement, elevator boarding softlock, store-entry bounce, map, pause and Konami. One package search used a prepared fixture position with guards removed. Prepared package/life counts exercised level clear, newspaper, post, loop 2, continue and game over. Gallery and CRT/mute toggles sampled, screenshots inspected. Isolated source-module probes confirmed the state, AI and input defects described above. No game JavaScript exception observed; favicon 404s. No published build or full-route completion.
